> Eventually, it may develop a more complete understanding of what was in the work

Sure, there's no doubt we can develop a better understanding of some of what he was talking about.

This is a long way from reconstructing the actual work itself into anything approximating the original work.

I'd encourage you to read eg https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.28170 for what is actually feasible in this area.

You're giving one of the more difficult cases, but here's how I suspect an LLM could meaningfully contribute

Take the portion covering 292–287 BC (the first missing book of his works, which we do have some fragments of).

If an LLM can figure out the following from surviving writings:

- When this book was published

- What sources Livy was using as references

- Which authors with surviving writings are known to have read Livy's writings, and what events from that period they talk about

Then perhaps it can comb through other surviving writing from writers in the 0-250 CE era who had access to Livy's work, and find even more sections referencing the missing work, which historians did not yet connect to that work (perhaps there are archives of surviving writings from that era which are digitized but not yet transcribed or translated due to being considered to have limited historical value). I'm also reminded of this story from early 2024 when an unreadable scroll was read with new digital forensics techniques for the first time: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=39261861

Eventually, it may develop a more complete understanding of what was in the work, which is defensible with references to other surviving (or recovered) works.

From there, perhaps it can recreate approximations of sections of the work. Maybe not the entire book in full right now. But parts of it with reasonable certainty of the contents at the very least.

> An example would be its complete inclusion in another book which analyzed the original text. Another example would be several surviving texts which each contain large selections of the original work, such that combining them would recreate the original work.

This is what is currently called "hallucination".

Yes, it can stitch the existing parts together, and provide reasonable summaries of parts that are described by other works.

But take Livy's Ab Urbe Condita: 35 out of the 142 books survive today. We have a rough idea what the others cover in terms of dates of nothing else (it is a history) but there are entire decades where we have no references to what he said.

In some cases there are major events that we can guess he might have written about, but it's a guess! There is just no way to know, and no LLM can fill in something that doesn't exist.

There are probably texts which were lost in the destruction of Alexandria which can be fully rebuilt from other quotes, without needing to use any inference (in the older sense of the word). An example would be its complete inclusion in another book which analyzed the original text. Another example would be several surviving texts which each contain large selections of the original work, such that combining them would recreate the original work.

This seems like the low-hanging fruit of the challenge. This is "simply" a task of LLMs combing all of humanity's archives to pick juicy needles out of haystacks (some of these surviving works may be quite obscure).

Next we have situations where perhaps 50% of a lost text can be reproduced via the above method, and an idea of what the remaining 50% can be obtained through analysis of contemporaneous texts which reference the original (without quoting it, or perhaps by paraphrasing, or giving a nod to), as well as a historical review of the life of the lost text's author (including the point in their life in which they wrote the lost work, and perhaps surviving lost works by them which came after) and their contemporaries.

In these situations, an approximation of what they might have written can be constructed, which IMO would be quite valuable. Perhaps each section which is filled in by an LLM could have notes containing supporting citations, assumptions which were made, and reasoning for those assumptions.

I'd love to see this put to the test by taking a work for which 50% of its text could be reconstructed from other works which cite it, then training a model on a corpus which is completely absent of the 50% which "would be lost" if constructed from the referencing works alone, then ask the model to generate the original text to the best of its abilities, including research capabilities (but with a classifier sitting between the model and any research results which would prevent it from "cheating" accidentally or otherwise)

The work generated from such an attempt at restoration could then be compared to the complete original work to explore the hypothesis. It actually reminds me a lot of the process through which some older paintings have been restored, when the original is incomplete.

This is a good example of reductio ad absurdum.

If "it's just more computation" can be used to dismiss AI achievements, the same logic can be used to dismiss human achievements next to animals.

Human and chicken brains are both made of neurons doing electrochemical signaling. The major difference is scale. Humans have ~86 billion neurons versus a few hundred million in a chicken, with some differences in how they're organized.
